rationale: The paused lead's bound can be settled from source even without the measurement it still needs, and doing so draws a distinction that matters for the report: in the running case the blocking send has a second arm on the shutdown channel, and a caller holding the Raft handle can close that channel, whereas the startup-replay deadlock happens before any handle exists. So the runtime stall is bounded by the FSM's own progress or by the caller shutting the node down, while the startup case has no such escape. This submission records that as a source-only part-answer and leaves the behavioural half of the question open.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only part-answer. The delivery of committed entries is a blocking select-send on a channel that nothing in the entry path times out or rejects, so once that channel is full the main loop waits until the FSM consumes a batch - the non-progress lasts exactly as long as the application's FSM lags behind its commits, and the library offers no deferral, no rejection and no queue growth. What bounds it is therefore the consumer and the caller, and both are reachable in the running case: the FSM makes progress whenever it applies, and a caller that already holds the Raft instance can shut the node down, because Shutdown closes the shutdown channel that the blocked send also selects on, which makes the batch respond ErrRaftShutdown and releases the main loop. That is precisely the escape the startup-replay finding lacks: there the same send blocks before NewRaft has returned, so no caller can hold a handle to close that channel, and the only reader is a goroutine the same constructor starts after the blocking call. The distinction is worth recording for the report because it is what makes the two cases different in kind rather than in degree, and it is drawn from the two anchors rather than from a run. The behavioural half of this question - whether a stalled main loop is long enough to matter, in that it stops processing RPCs and its own lease check while commits continue - still needs the harness described in the discriminator, so the claim here stays unresolved rather than asserted.

knowledge.assertion: The entry says the library transfers the FSM's latency into the main loop by a blocking send with no rejection path; this reading adds that the same select has a shutdown arm, so a caller holding the handle can release it.

counterevidence: The shutdown arm bounds the stall only for a caller that holds the handle and chooses to stop the node; it is not a repair for the cluster, which loses that node.
The FSM's own progress is the only other bound, and it depends entirely on the application, which is why the question's behavioural half cannot be settled by reading.
No measurement was made for this question, so nothing here says how long a stall lasts in practice or how it interacts with the leader's lease in a real cluster.
limitations: This is a source-only part-answer that leaves the question open rather than a finding.
The shutdown-path claim rests on the select in the FSM delivery and on Shutdown closing that channel; the run never exercised a shutdown during a full channel.
The relationship to the startup-replay finding is an argument from structure, not a comparison of two executions.
